text: Behind your wall is a wire that could start a fire. One small switch stops it.
A circuit breaker. Just metal, a magnet, and a spring.
Current heats wire. Too much, and the insulation melts, then burns.
Every circuit has a limit, usually fifteen or twenty amps. The breaker cuts power before the wire overheats.
Defense one: a strip of two metals bonded together. Brass, and steel.
Current heats the strip. Brass expands more, so it bends.
Bend far enough, and it knocks a latch loose. A spring snaps the contacts open.
But heat is slow. A short circuit sends thousands of amps in a blink.
Defense two: an electromagnet. A surge creates a magnetic pull that trips the latch instantly.
That's the trip curve. A small overload gets minutes. A huge one, milliseconds.
When one trips, unplug what was running, then switch it fully off, and back on.
Trips again? Call an electrician. Never tape it down, or swap in a bigger breaker.
Watch again, and catch the moment the strip bends.
